planting.note: Start transplants or plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; rock penstemon is adapted to limestone cliffs and ledges and rots quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil.

directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; rock penstemon is adapted to limestone cliffs and ledges and rots quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil. Small, glossy, evergreen leaves clothe woody-based stems that form a low, shrubby mound, studded from summer into fall with tubular, bright red-orange flowers that are outstanding hummingbird forage during a season when many other penstemons have finished blooming. Native to limestone canyon walls and rocky slopes of the Trans-Pecos and Edwards Plateau regions of Texas into northern Mexico, it is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant penstemons available, thriving in the reflected heat of a rock garden or dry stone wall. Established plants need no supplemental water beyond natural rainfall and benefit from a light trim after the main flowering flush to keep the mound tidy.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or plant transplants, into sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed catchfly is native to open pine savannas and sandy roadsides and prefers lean soil over rich garden beds.

directions: Direct sow after last frost, or plant transplants, into sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed catchfly is native to open pine savannas and sandy roadsides and prefers lean soil over rich garden beds. Slender, sticky-hairy stems bear narrow leaves and clusters of vivid red, deeply fringed, tubular flowers in late summer and fall, opening in the evening to attract nectaring sphinx moths and hummingbirds. Native to open longleaf pine woodlands and sandy prairies across the western Gulf coastal plain, it is a striking, little-known addition to a native pollinator garden that provides late-season color when few other wildflowers are still fresh. It self-sows in loose, sandy soil and needs no fertilizer, performing best in the same lean, well-drained conditions it favors in the wild.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; dwarf wild indigo develops a long taproot like other baptisias and transplants poorly once established, so choose its permanent location carefully.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; dwarf wild indigo develops a long taproot like other baptisias and transplants poorly once established, so choose its permanent location carefully. This compact prairie native carries blue-green, clover-like foliage and short spikes of violet-blue, pea-shaped flowers in mid-spring, followed by dark, rattling seed pods that add interest into fall and winter, all on a plant that stays notably lower and tidier than larger baptisia species. Native to rocky prairies and open woodlands of the south-central plains, it is a long-lived, drought-tolerant nitrogen-fixer well suited to the front of a native perennial border where taller wild indigos would be out of scale. It requires no division or fertilizing and, once established, tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; prairie golden-pea forms a deep taproot and spreads slowly by rhizome once established, so allow it room to naturalize.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; prairie golden-pea forms a deep taproot and spreads slowly by rhizome once established, so allow it room to naturalize. One of the earliest prairie wildflowers to bloom, it sends up short spikes of bright yellow, pea-shaped flowers in early spring — historically noted by settlers and Indigenous peoples as one of the first signs of the growing season on the northern plains, appearing around the time bison calves ('buffalo') were born. Silvery-green, three-parted leaves persist after bloom, and the plant spreads gradually by rhizome to form loose colonies in native prairie and rangeland restorations. It is extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, needing no irrigation or fertilizer, and its nitrogen-fixing roots benefit surrounding prairie soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; golden dalea forms a deep taproot typical of prairie clovers and is best planted while young rather than transplanted later.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; golden dalea forms a deep taproot typical of prairie clovers and is best planted while young rather than transplanted later. Silvery, silky-haired stems and finely divided gray-green leaflets set off dense, cylindrical spikes of golden-yellow flowers in summer, a color unusual among the mostly purple- and white-flowered prairie clovers, drawing bees and small butterflies to prairies and dry rangeland across the southern Great Plains. Like other daleas, it fixes nitrogen and thrives on the poor, dry, sandy or rocky soils where richer garden plants struggle, making it a valuable, low-maintenance addition to a xeriscape or native prairie planting. It needs no irrigation once established and tolerates heavy grazing or mowing by resprouting from its deep root crown.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; black dalea is a limestone-adapted Texas shrub that thrives on neglect and rots in rich, moist, or heavily irrigated soil.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; black dalea is a limestone-adapted Texas shrub that thrives on neglect and rots in rich, moist, or heavily irrigated soil. Fine, wiry, blue-green foliage clothes a low, rounded, woody-based shrub that bursts into bloom in fall with masses of small, rich reddish-purple to violet flowers with contrasting yellow anthers, providing an important late-season nectar source for bees just as many other xeriscape plants are finishing. Native to limestone hills and caliche flats across central and west Texas into Mexico, it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established and requires no supplemental irrigation, fertilizer, or pruning beyond an occasional light shaping. Its fine texture and fall color make it a valuable structural component of a Texas-style xeriscape or native pollinator planting.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, scarifying seed to speed germination, into sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining vines to climb; spurred butterfly pea tolerates poor, dry soil and needs no fertilizer.

directions: Direct sow after last frost, scarifying seed to speed germination, into sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining vines to climb; spurred butterfly pea tolerates poor, dry soil and needs no fertilizer. Slender, twining stems carry trifoliate leaves and showy, flattened, lavender-to-purple, pea-shaped flowers with a distinctive spurred keel from summer into fall, scrambling over low shrubs and fences or trailing as a groundcover where no support is available. Native to sandy pinelands, dunes, and open woodland edges across the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain, it is a larval host and nectar source for several native bee and butterfly species and fixes nitrogen in the lean, sandy soils it favors. It behaves as a perennial in zones 8-10 and dies back to the root in occasional hard freezes, resprouting readily from its woody crown the following spring.
